signals.excerpt:
MiniMax-M3.1 on AMD Instinct GPUs

# MiniMax-M3.1 on AMD Instinct GPUs: Day-0 support and optimization

 Oct 22, 2026

## TL;DR

- MiniMax-M3.1, MiniMax’s natively multimodal MoE model for coding and agent workloads (1M-token context, NVFP4 experts, a DSpark speculative-decoding draft), serves on AMD Instinct™ MI350 GPUs with both vLLM and ATOM on day 0.
- An MXFP4 checkpoint produced with AMD Quark, and an equivalent load-time conversion of the NVFP4 checkpoint, run the routed experts on AITER’s MXFP4 fused-MoE kernels; accuracy on both matches within the evaluation error on GSM8K, AIME and MMMU-Pro.
- vLLM: mono decode, one fused kernel launch per MoE layer for the whole decode step, cuts the per-token decode latency 3.2x at one request, 2.1x at four and 1.5x at sixteen compared with the same server with mono decode off, and gives 2.2-2.4x the interactivity on real coding-agent traces at 1-8 concurrent users.
- vLLM: DSpark speculative decoding composes with mono decode and adds about a third more interactivity at 1-4 users and 13% at 8; on its own it is the fallback where mono decode cannot run.
- ATOM: per-channel FP8 attention and a fused shared expert are applied at start-up, and the DSpark draft pass is CUDA-graph captured, accepting about half of its 7 drafts on real text.
- Serving commands for both engines and both checkpoints, for latency-bound (few users) and throughput-bound (many users) deployments, and for agentic workloads, are given in each engine’s section.

...

## Introduction

We are excited to announce Day-0 support for MiniMax-M3.1 on AMD Instinct™ MI350 Series GPUs across the AMD inference software stack: the ROCm™ build of vLLM and ATOM, the AMD inference engine, both running on ROCm with AITER kernels, with an MXFP4 checkpoint produced by AMD Quark. MiniMax-M3.1 is MiniMax’s latest natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model for coding and agent workloads, with a 1M-token context, built-in reasoning with selectable effort, native tool calling and a DSpark speculative-decoding draft.

...

## Day 0 support for AMD Instinct GPUs

MiniMax-M3.1 is supported on AMD Instinct MI350 Series GPUs in both inference engines from day 0: vLLM and ATOM. Both run the routed experts on AITER’s MXFP4 fused MoE with fp8 KV and index caches, AITER’s INT4 quick-reduce for the all-reduces, and tensor parallelism over 4 GPUs per model replica, so two replicas fit on an 8-GPU node. vLLM serves both checkpoints below (the MiniMax-M3.1-Flash release with its experts converted at load, and the Quark MXFP4 export); ATOM serves the Quark MXFP4 export. Where the two engines differ is in how they treat the MXFP8 attention linears and the shared expert at start-up, described in each engine’s section.

...

## Accuracy

Evaluated with lm-eval against the running server, per engine and checkpoint. GSM8K on the full 1,319-question test set (5-shot chat with the few-shot turns as prior chat turns, flexible / strict match); AIME 2025 and AIME 2026 as mean@16 (16 seeded passes, temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95); MMMU-Pro standard and vision splits (vision tower on). The vLLM rows were served with recipe 1 and recipe 2 above (mono decode + DSpark draft, maximum reasoning effort); the ATOM rows with the ATOM commands above (the accuracy-first row is PTPC attention with the shared expert kept as a separate MXFP8 MLP, with DSpark).

# Democratizing reliable knowledge-seeking with MyGPT: a privacy-first, open-source retrieval-augmented generation platform

## Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) have transformed knowledge discovery, but their use in sensitive domains is limited by privacy concerns and risks of data leakage. Moreover, LLMs may hallucinate when queried about information outside their training data, undermining their reliability for scientific, clinical, or policy-related tasks. We present MyGPT, a fully open-source, privacy-preserving retrieval-augmented-generation (RAG) platform that uses open-source LLMs and operates locally or within secure institutional environments. MyGPT empowers users to query user-defined libraries such as biomedical literature, confidential clinical documents, and multilingual global health policies, while ensuring that sensitive data never leaves the secure environment. We introduce confidence metrics, including “relevance scores” and “hallucination index,” and provide explicit source citation from the library within a single interface to assess contextual support for generated answers. MyGPT offers a cost-effective, modular, open-source alternative to commercial LLM services and democratizes knowledge-seeking across multiple domains, including use at remote facilities without internet access.

signals.title: Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 1 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 1 | NVIDIA Technical Blog

# Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 1

 Oct 23, 2026 

 By Jian Hu and Lin Chai 

 AI-Generated Summary 

- NVIDIA TensorRT builds inference engines by making interdependent scheduling decisions across graph transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization.
- A mathematical framework models compilation as a builder algorithm generating candidate solutions and a searching algorithm selecting the fastest feasible one under accuracy constraints.
- The Global Performance Tuner, released in TensorRT 11.1, introduces customizable build routes that expand the solution space and validate each candidate against end-to-end accuracy and performance.
- Three principles guide the tuner: accuracy-aware tuning, customizable build routes, and a large solution space from which the fastest acceptable engine is selected.

...

Deploying a trained neural network involves more than translating each operator into a GPU kernel. It is a compilation problem with many legitimate answers. For example, when NVIDIA TensorRT builds an engine, it makes interdependent decisions about graph-IR transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization. This process is called scheduling. Different scheduling choices can preserve model semantics yet produce very different inference performance, making scheduling central to deep learning compiler optimization.

No single scheduling strategy is best for every model and deployment environment. A transformation that accelerates one network may slow another. A kernel that is faster in isolation may interact poorly with fusion, tensor layouts, or memory traffic elsewhere in the graph. Aggressive scheduling may improve performance while violating an application’s accuracy requirement. These coupled, model-dependent effects often appear only after the complete engine is built and measured, making the right strategy increasingly difficult to predict.

This post is Part 1 of a two-part series that is intended to develop a clearer way of reasoning about performance optimization. It explores questions such as: What makes one compiled engine better than another? Why can individually promising decisions fail end to end? How should accuracy constrain performance optimization? It introduces the Global Performance Tuner, a feature for automatic performance tuning released in TensorRT 11.1, and explores these questions through an intuitive example and mathematical framework.

...

The Global Performance Tuner begins with the idea of customizable build routes. For each candidate solution, it validates the outputs against the specified accuracy criterion and measures end-to-end inference performance. Among all solutions that meet accuracy requirements, the searching algorithm selects the minimum-runtime feasible solution from the expanded solution set.

The following three principles define the framework:

- Accuracy-aware tuning: Use end-to-end accuracy as a constraint that guides performance tuning.
- Customizable build route: Make build routes customizable so that scheduling can adapt to each model and deployment environment.
- Large solution space: Construct a rich feasible solution set, then select the fastest candidate whose numerical difference remains within the specified tolerance.

signals.title: The science behind TorchNeuron, Amazon’s new PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium chips - Amazon Science
signals.excerpt:
# The science behind TorchNeuron, Amazon’s new PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium chips 

## Runtime optimizations and a thorough evaluation process driven by agentic AI help ensure that models written in PyTorch will execute efficiently and reliably on Trainium systems.

 By Robert Hundt, Arash Jamalian, Apoorv Gupta, Charan Shettyhalli Guruswamy, Abigail Fernandes, Rui Silva, Adarsh Singh, Sarang Ozarde , Khaled ElGalaind, Maen Suleiman

 October 22, 2026 

 Key takeaways 

- TorchNeuron, Amazon's open-source PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, used AI agents to narrow hundreds of thousands of Hugging Face models down to 841 representative models for tuning and benchmarking
- Caching and shared-compilation optimizations cut time to the first training step by about a third on a large language model shared across accelerators
- Its opt-in "adaptive eager" mode overlaps compile time with execution to approach fully compiled performance without the overhead

...

This week, we announced the availability of TorchNeuron, an open-source backend that translates PyTorch code into operations executable on AWS Trainium systems. PyTorch code that already runs on other accelerators will run on Trainium with minimal or no code changes.

TorchNeuron bridges PyTorch and Trainium, and both sides gain from it. PyTorch developers can now run their code on Trainium, which was built from the ground up for large-tensor workloads. They can also tap the AWS Neuron SDK, which includes a profiler that traces each instruction with cycle-level accuracy and the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI, pronounced "Nikki"), which enables control almost at the assembly level.

TorchNeuron enables seamless integration between PyTorch models, the AWS Neuron SDK, and AWS Trainium chips.

TorchNeuron includes several optimizations that enable PyTorch code to run efficiently on Trainium, including caching at multiple levels and an optional “adaptive eager” mode that doesn’t execute individual operations one by one, as is typical in plain eager mode, but instead groups and compiles operations for more efficient execution, approaching fully compiled performance.

Much of the innovation behind TorchNeuron, however, is the way its performance was evaluated. AI agents searched through hundreds of thousands of open-source models and categorized them according to their architectural characteristics. This allowed the Annapurna team around Khaled ElGalaind and Sarang Ozarde to identify 841 representative models covering the full spectrum of model architectures. From those models, they also distilled tens of thousands of practically important tensor dimensions, or “shapes”, which were then used to tune and benchmark TorchNeuron’s performance. The result is that PyTorch programmers can trust TorchNeuron to execute their code accurately, efficiently, and most importantly, right out of the box.

...

In a distributed training setup, caching also leverages all processes participating in the run. Processes that run the same part of the model need the same NEFFs, so on a single machine, dozens of them may ask for identical compiled code. TorchNeuron runs a shared compilation service so that each operation is compiled only once per machine, and the other processes reuse the result, without overwhelming the host CPUs. In tests with a large language model spread across 64 processes on a single machine, the service cut the time to the first training step by about a third.

signals.title: Introducing Infinity: a runtime for extreme agent concurrency | AWS Open Source Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Introducing Infinity: a runtime for extreme agent concurrency

by Shadaj Laddad on 23 OCT 2026 in Announcements Permalink Share

Agents spend much of their time waiting on tools. A coding agent may start a build that runs for twenty minutes, a triage agent may wait hours for the next pull request on a repository, and an assistant may wait until the next morning for an approval. Most agent harnesses run the agent loop as a sequence of blocking steps: the harness calls the model, invokes a tool, waits for the tool to return, and repeats. While the agent waits, it holds a process and its memory, and it cannot respond to events that arrive in the meantime.

Today, we’re releasing Infinity under the Apache 2.0 open source license as part of the Hydro project, a collaborative effort between AWS and UC Berkeley. Infinity is a research project that re-imagines agent runtimes, based on the techniques that programming languages use to suspend and resume asynchronous functions. When an agent calls a tool, Infinity dispatches the call, saves the conversation, and suspends the agent. When the tool result arrives, the runtime resumes the agent from its saved state.

With Infinity, concurrent agents are extremely lightweight. For example, we can fit 75,000 concurrent agents in the 8 GB of a Raspberry Pi 5. Infinity also makes it possible to deploy concurrent agents on standard serverless platforms. When Infinity suspends an agent during a tool call, the serverless function can end. So even if a tool call takes days, nothing needs to run while the agent waits.

signals.title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last | MIT Technology Review
signals.excerpt:
Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management, scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability.

For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it.

...

### Engineer the system, not the model

Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency.

Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance.

GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model's weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive.

The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize. Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat.

...

EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable.

signals.excerpt:
# Meta Releases Wonder, Opens Spark All about Muse Wonder (API), Muse Wonder Full (subscription), and Muse Spark Open (weights available)

Published Oct 23, 2026

Meta marched all the way back to the AI frontier to offer a Muse model for everyone: a high-end agentic model (comparable to Claude Sonnet 5.5) that costs $50 per month to access, its moderately-priced sibling (comparable to GPT-6.1 Sol), and an open model that outperforms any yet released by a company outside China.

What’s new: Meta made three multimodal models available in one week, including the top-of-the-line Muse Wonder Full, the multimodal Muse Wonder, and the locally deployable Muse Spark Open. Muse Wonder is available via API and Muse Spark Open’s weights are free to download, but Muse Wonder Full is only available to Muse Code subscribers.

- Input/output: Text, image, video, and audio in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens), 139 tokens/second (Muse Wonder) and 143 tokens/second (Muse Spark Open)
- Architecture: Mixture-of-experts transformer, 816 billion parameters, 42 billion active per token, 256 experts (Muse Spark Open)
- Features: Six reasoning levels (minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max), reasoning always on, tool calling, structured outputs
- Performance: Tied for second on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index (56, Muse Wonder Full); seventh (52, Muse Wonder); seventh among open weight models, first among U.S. open models (39, Muse Spark Open)
- Availability: API and subscription (Muse Wonder), subscription only (Muse Wonder Full), weights available via Meta and Hugging Face (Muse Spark Open)
- Price: $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens (Muse Wonder); $50/month (Muse Wonder Full); $1.25/$4.15 input/output (Muse Spark Open)
- Weights/license: Weights for Muse Spark Open available under the Muse Model license, which allows for commercial and noncommercial use for up to $20 million of revenue; display of “Built with Muse Spark Open” required for products and services using the model; separate licenses available for other users; Muse Wonder and Wonder Full are proprietary
- Undisclosed: Knowledge cutoff, parameters and architecture for Muse Wonder models, specific training datasets and methods

...

Performance: Muse Wonder Full is the top-performing of the three models, two points behind Claude Opus 5.5 and identical with Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index. Muse Spark Open is the top open weights model outside China, ahead of Mistral Large 4 and Reflection’s Beam. Its Intelligence Index average is identical with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash’s, but is still behind MiMo-V.2.6-Pro’s and GLM-5.3’s.

- On AA’s Intelligence Index, a weighted average of ten independent benchmarks, Muse Wonder Full achieved a 56, Muse Wonder a 52, and Muse Spark Open a 39. Meta’s former flagship model, Muse Spark 1.3, achieved an average of 48.
- Muse Wonder costs $4.52 per Intelligence Index task, fifth highest among current models; Wonder Full’s cost per task cannot be measured, since it’s not available via API. Muse Spark Open costs $0.84 per task, more than GPT-6.1 Sol, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. 
- Artificial Analysis notes Muse Wonder and Wonder Full’s low knowledge marks but also partly offset this through their low hallucination rates. On the AA-Omniscience Index, Muse Wonder Full (30) and Wonder (25) place 8th and 10th respectively.
- Muse Spark Open only requires about 1 TB of memory at 4-bit precision. This means it can be run locally on 2 Mac Studios with 512 GB of memory each (or 4 with 256 GB, etc.). Meta and Apple touted their work together to make the model capable of running on Apple’s consumer-grade silicon.

signals.title: RAGFlow Just Updated: Agentic AI Gets a Major Upgrade as Go Rewrites Reshape the RAG Platform - UNDERCODE NEWS
signals.excerpt:
By Humanoid Deep Analyser / 2 days ago 

RAGFlow Pushes Toward a More Powerful, Lightweight AI Knowledge Platform

RAGFlow is moving toward a more capable and streamlined architecture with its v1.0.0-rc2 release candidate. The open-source retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) platform combines document parsing, knowledge-base management, semantic search, and AI-powered answers to help organizations build assistants grounded in their own data.

The second release candidate builds on the substantial architectural changes introduced in v1.0.0-rc1. Rather than focusing on a single feature, this update improves agentic AI, expands integration options, consolidates document-processing infrastructure, and fixes issues uncovered during the first release candidate.

The result is a platform moving closer to its planned 1.0 release, although rc2 remains a release candidate rather than a guarantee of final production stability.

Agentic Mode Replaces the Old Thinking-Level Controls

One of the most visible changes is the introduction of Agentic mode for chat, replacing the previous Low, Medium, High, and Ultra thinking-level options.

This change reflects a broader shift in AI application design. Instead of presenting users with a simple choice of reasoning intensity, RAGFlow is moving toward a more agent-oriented interaction model in which AI can coordinate retrieval and other operations to produce answers.

The update also includes work to port agentic RAG into Go and expose it as a chat mode, alongside per-dialog failover. This is significant because retrieval-heavy AI systems need to do more than generate fluent text: they must locate relevant evidence, process it reliably, and recover gracefully when individual operations fail.

However, the release notes do not establish that Agentic mode will outperform every previous thinking level in every workload. Its practical value will depend on the models, retrieval configuration, datasets, and tasks involved.

...

More Model Providers and Search Integrations Expand Flexibility

RAGFlow is also widening the range of external services that can participate in its AI workflows.

signals.excerpt:
# NVIDIA TensorRT dramatically accelerates Stable Diffusion 3.5 on RTX GPUs

14 June 2025, 23:26· 1 min read

The rise of generative artificial intelligence models has transformed digital creativity but also increased hardware demands, especially for VRAM. Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large, a leading image generation model, originally required over 18GB of VRAM, restricting its usability to only a handful of high-end systems. NVIDIA has addressed this limitation by collaborating with Stability AI to quantize the model to FP8—a process that trims VRAM usage by 40%, making it possible for more systems to run the model effectively.

This optimization, combined with the power of NVIDIA TensorRT, generates significant performance leaps. TensorRT, NVIDIA’s AI inference platform, has been reengineered for RTX AI PCs and now offers just-in-time, on-device engine building. Alongside reduced VRAM use, quantized Stable Diffusion 3.5 models see performance more than double, with FP8 TensorRT delivering a 2.3x speedup and 40% lower memory use compared to baseline PyTorch implementations in BF16. Medium versions are also optimized, with a 1.7x increase in speed. These advances allow image creation and editing tasks to proceed quickly and in real time, even on RTX GPUs with less VRAM.

TensorRT for RTX is now available as a standalone software development kit, letting developers take advantage of rapid JIT engine creation without the need for training on device-specific packages. The SDK is eight times smaller than before and integrates with Windows ML for streamlined deployment. The optimized Stable Diffusion 3.5 models are live on Hugging Face and will soon be accessible as NVIDIA NIM microservices, further simplifying deployment for developers and creatives. Such coordinated advances mark a vital step in democratizing high-performance generative artificial intelligence, making advanced image synthesis accessible on a much wider range of systems.

signals.excerpt:

Discover Summary

## Automatic Search Feature Introduced in TensorRT 11.1

NVIDIA has introduced a global performance tuner in TensorRT 11.1 that automatically searches and compares multiple build paths for AI inference engines. The feature generates build paths from combinations of compiler settings, then builds an engine for each path and measures overall inference performance.

The command-line tool `trtexec` expands search conditions into individual build paths and evaluates candidate engines in sequence. Candidates that fail to build or do not meet the specified accuracy criteria are excluded, and the path with the highest measured performance among the remaining engines is selected.

...

## Up to 1.63x Improvement Across 10 Workloads

In NVIDIA’s published comparison across 10 workloads, tuned paths delivered performance of 1.14–1.63x that of each workload’s default build path. These figures are results for the workloads included in the comparison and do not mean that the same performance gains are guaranteed for all models.

TensorRT 11.1 allows users to adjust more than 200 settings. These settings affect compiler choices, including heuristics, operation fusion, and code generation methods. The tuner measures the completed engine as a whole, rather than individual operations, to find a path suited to the model and execution environment.

signals.title: Deepseek's latest AI model is smarter than ever, but its low running costs come at a price — uses only one-quarter of the HBM and one-eighth of SSD storage but still battles hallucinations in agentic workloads | Tom's Hardware
signals.excerpt:
Deepseek just upgraded its V4.1 Flash open-weight model to revision 1017. What looks like a mere point revision may actually be a significant step forward in model efficiency. On the product page, Deepseek uses the slogan "wish-driven programming made real," a likely reference to the colloquial "vibe coding," implying the model is a good fit for open-ended tasks with broad descriptions. However, while the model is indeed cheap and scores well, it can be hallucination-prone.

LLMs are roughly divided into two categories: closed commercial efforts from frontier labs, whose models are expensive to run but deliver excellent results, and Chinese open-weight competitors that broadly exchange reliability for a much cheaper running cost, particularly for long-running agentic tasks.

Deepseek V4.1 Flash (DSF) is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 552B total parameters, 16B of which are active during runs. The model is multimodal, accepts both text and images as inputs, and its context window length measures the now-standard 1 million tokens.

According to Deepseek's internal benchmarks, the model slots in neatly between GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5, even beating Anthropic's LLM in task tests. That's already a strong showing, but this latest revision of DSF shines in the performance-per-task base and token efficiency. The upgrade from V4 Flash to V4.1 Flash significantly slashed hardware requirements, with V4.1 using only one-quarter of the HBM and one-eighth of SSD storage for its KV cache compared to its predecessor, spending only 890 bytes per token entry.

...

DeepSWE isn't the only benchmark around, either. Artificial Analysis ranks DSF-1017 (max) as only #2 on its intelligence index within the large open-weight class, with a score of 45. For reference, the most seemingly intelligent model, Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback), rings in at 58. It's one of the fastest models in its category, too, and its cost-per-task is edged out only by Xiaomi's MiMo V2.6-Pro.

This all sounds too good to be true, but everyone knows the adage of "fast, cheap, and reliable, pick two." So what's the catch? In one word: hallucination. Just because a model is smart doesn't mean it's reliable. Broadly speaking, users prefer models that don't answer when they lack supporting facts, and DSF-1017 doesn't seem very good at knowing what it doesn't know.

Artificial Analysis' Omniscience benchmark is quite clear on this matter, ranking the model among the lowest. It answered questions correctly 43% of the time, which is among the best for open-weight models, but inferior to the proprietary competition. That would be perfectly acceptable if it skipped answers without a foundation, but it hallucinated 67% of non-answers.

The benchmark's main index grants points for good answers and deducts them for wrong ones, and non-answers don't count. DSF-1017 gets 5 points, compared to Kimi K3-max's 20, with the frontier models coming in at 42+. Ultimately, this means DFS-1017 is by no means incompetent — much the opposite —but one should be careful about which tasks to assign to the model.

signals.title: TanStack AI 1.0 Is Here: Use Cases, Strengths and the Experimental Harness | sAIgnals
signals.excerpt:
# TanStack AI 1.0 Is Here: Use Cases, Strengths and the Experimental Harness

TanStack [released TanStack AI 1.0 on October 23](https://tanstack.com/blog/tanstack-ai-1-0). It is a TypeScript toolkit for adding AI features to an application—not a new language model or a hosted inference service. The **core APIs are now stable**; the newly announced **agent harness is experimental**. That distinction matters if you are deciding what to ship to production.

...

## What does TanStack AI do?

The [overview](https://tanstack.com/ai/latest/docs/getting-started/overview) describes a server-side adapter that calls a model provider and a client hook that reads streamed responses. The SDK covers streaming chat, tool calling, and media generation. TanStack says 1.0 includes 23 provider adapters and UI integrations spanning React, Vue, Solid, Svelte and other frameworks. That lets a TypeScript app keep its own UI and swap model adapters without rewriting the whole chat flow; adapter support and model-specific capabilities still need checking. [Source: release announcement](https://tanstack.com/blog/tanstack-ai-1-0)

...

Three concrete use cases:

1. **A support or documentation assistant inside an existing app.** Stream answers into a custom UI, add typed tools for permitted account or knowledge-base lookups, and require approval before sensitive tool actions. [Source: overview and tools](https://tanstack.com/ai/latest/docs/getting-started/overview) 2. **A multi-provider workflow.** Keep the app’s chat and tool structure while evaluating another provider adapter for a specific task, such as lower-latency summaries or image generation. That is an integration option, not a promise that every model behaves identically. [Source: overview](https://tanstack.com/ai/latest/docs/getting-started/overview) 3. **A long response that survives a dropped connection.** TanStack’s [resumable streams](https://tanstack.com/ai/latest/docs/resumable-streams/overview) log chunks for replay on reconnect without another model call. The quickstart’s in-memory adapter is for development or a single process; production deployments need a shared durability backend. Conversation persistence is a separate concern.

...

## Where might it be stronger than Vercel AI SDK?

Both are open-source TypeScript toolkits that stream chat and call tools across providers. According to [TanStack’s own comparison](https://tanstack.com/ai/latest/docs/comparison/vercel-ai-sdk), its differentiators include the open **AG-UI** wire protocol, per-model TypeScript option narrowing, one tool schema that can run server-side or client-side, and its composable durability path. These can be real advantages when an app must interoperate with AG-UI agents, own its UI, or resume streams across network drops. They are **architectural differences documented by TanStack, not independent evidence that TanStack is faster, cheaper, or more accurate**.

...

## What is stable—and what is not?

TanStack says the 1.0 core is production-ready, but `@tanstack/ai-harness` and related harness entry points remain experimental 0.x APIs and may change in minor releases. The harness aims to keep an agent session alive across messages and deployment boundaries, including coding-agent workflows. Treat it as a prototype candidate, not part of the 1.0 stability promise. [Source: launch post](https://tanstack.com/blog/tanstack-ai-1-0)
